# Fourier Analysis

::: {.callout-important title="Definition of Fourier Transform"}

Let $u$ be a function that consumes a real-valued number and maps it to a complex-valued number. Mathematically, $u: \mathbb R\to\mathbb C$. Then its Fourier transform $\hat u(\omega)$ is defined by the following formula.

$$
\hat u(\omega)=\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,\mathrm dx
$$ {#eq-fourier-transform}

The Fourier inversion formula recovers the original $u(x)$ in @eq-fourier-transform from a given $\hat u(\omega)$.

$$
u(x)=\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\hat u(\omega)e^{i\omega x}\,\mathrm dx
$$ {#eq-fourier-inversion-formula}

:::

**Remarks:**

1. The function $\hat u(\omega)$ will generally be a complex-valued function even if $u(x)$ is a strictly real-valued function.

2. The definition given above is not that rigorous.

For completeness, the Fourier transform of an arbitrary example is given below.

::: {.callout-note title="Fourier Transform Example" collapse=true}

Let's apply @eq-fourier-transform to compute $\hat u(\omega)$ if $u(x)$ is defined as the discontinuous function below.

$$
u(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-x} & x\geq0 \\0 & x<0\end{cases}
$$

By @eq-fourier-transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat u(\omega) & =\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,\mathrm dx\\ & =\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^{\infty}e^{-x}e^{-i\omega x}\,\mathrm dx\\ & =\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac 1{1+i\omega}
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

The Fourier transform definition above assumed $u(x)$ was an analytical function. Now, we give a definition for a grid function $v$.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition of Discrete Fourier Transform"}

Let $v$ be a function defined on the grid as $v:h\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$, then the Fourier transform of the discrete grid function $v$ is

$$
\hat v(\xi)=\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum\limits_{m\in\mathbb Z}v_me^{-imh\xi}h
$$ {#eq-discrete-fourier-transform}

The infinite sum in the discrete case can be viewed as a Riemann sum approximation of the integral in @eq-fourier-transform. The Fourier-transformed function $\hat v(\xi)$ is indeed a function defined on $\mathbb C$. However, it is also helpful to view it as a periodic function. As we will show later, $\hat v(\xi)$ is indeed periodic with period $\frac {2\pi}h$ due to $e^{-imh\xi}$. When defining the discrete Fourier inversion formula, we must then restrict $\xi\in\left[-\frac {\pi}h,\frac {\pi}h\right]$ to ensure a well-defined inverse mapping.

$$
v_m=\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\pi/h}^{\pi/h}\hat v(\xi)e^{imh\xi}\,\mathrm d\xi
$$ {#eq-discrete-fourier-inversion-formula}

:::

**Remarks:** Instead of viewing $\hat v(\xi)$ as a function only on a finite interval, we can also interpret it as a $\frac {2\pi}h$-periodic function defined for all $\xi\in\mathbb R$. The reasoning for this comes from the $e^{-imh\xi}$ term, which itself is $\frac {2\pi}h$-periodic. From @eq-discrete-fourier-transform

$$
\hat v\left(\xi+\frac {2\pi}h\right)=\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum\limits_{m\in\mathbb Z}v_me^{-imh\left(x+\frac {2\pi}h\right)}h=\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum\limits_{m\in\mathbb Z}v_me^{-imh\xi}he^{-2\pi im}=\hat v(\xi)
$$

We next give a useful theorem in Fourier analysis.

::: {#thm-parsevals-relation}

## Parseval's Relation

For an integrable continuous function $u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$, the L^2^ norm of $u$ is equal to its Fourier-transformed counterpart.

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left|u(x)\right|^2\,\mathrm dx=\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\lVert\hat u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left|\hat u(\omega)\right|^2\,\mathrm d\omega
$$ {#eq-parsevals-relation}

Similarly, if $v$ is a grid-level function such that $v:h\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$, then the $h$-norm of $v$ is equal to the $h$-norm of its Fourier-transformed function.

$$
\sum\limits_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\left|v_m\right|^2h=\lVert v\rVert_h^2=\lVert\hat v\rVert_h^2=\int_{-\pi/h}^{\pi/h}\left|\hat v(\xi)\right|^2\,\mathrm d\xi
$$ {#eq-discrete-parsevals-relation}

:::

We give a nonrigorous proof of @eq-discrete-parsevals-relation. The proof of @eq-parsevals-relation may be found in another textbook.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof of Discrete Parseval's Relation" collapse=true}

From $\left|v_m\right|^2=\overline{\hat v(\xi)}\hat v(\xi)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lVert\hat v\rVert_h^2=\int_{-\pi/h}^{\pi/h}\overline{\hat v(\xi)}\hat v(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi & =\int_{-\pi/h}^{\pi/h}\frac {\overline{\hat v(\xi)}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum\limits_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}v_me^{-imh\xi}h\,\mathrm d\xi \\
 & =\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum\limits_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\pi/h}^{\pi/h}\overline{\hat v(\xi)}e^{-imh\xi}\,\mathrm d\xi\, v_mh \\
 & =\sum\limits_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\overline{\frac 1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\pi/h}^{\pi/h}\hat v(\xi)e^{imh\xi}\,\mathrm d\xi}\,v_mh \\
 & =\sum\limits_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\overline{v_m}v_mh \\
 & =\lVert v\rVert_h^2
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
